title: The Web Goes Public
tagline: Dial-up tones, home pages and new online shops.

locale.persona: a college student going online from the family PC

morningRoutine.detail: Online services still charged by the hour; AOL only switched to a flat monthly rate in December 1996.

places.title: The front page
places.description: Newspapers were still the main source of news, selling about 58 million copies each weekday. 1995 brought tragedy in Oklahoma City, a record stock market and a new version of Windows.
places.imageAlt: An early news web page in a browser window with blue underlined links
highlights: Bombing destroys the federal building in Oklahoma City
Dow closes above 5,000 for the first time

technology.description: eBay began as AuctionWeb on September 3, 1995.

technology.description: Went on sale in North America on September 9, 1995, at $299.

technology.name: Dial-up modem
technology.description: Modems on the phone line connected at up to 28.8 kbit/s under a standard approved in 1994; many older ones ran at 14.4 kbit/s.

futureVisions.prediction: "No online database will replace your daily newspaper", and online catalogue shopping won't make stores obsolete.
futureVisions.whoSaidIt: Clifford Stoll, "The Internet? Bah!", Newsweek, February 1995
futureVisions.note: U.S. daily newspaper circulation fell from about 58 million on weekdays in 1995 to 21 million in 2022, print and digital combined.

source.label: Clifford Stoll, "Why the Web Won't Be Nirvana" ("The Internet? Bah!"), Newsweek, posted 26 February 1995

futureVisions.prediction: The Internet and the World Wide Web are only a subset of a larger "information highway".
futureVisions.note: Streaming, online shopping and mobile internet went far beyond the 1995 web.
